I’ve asked some of the guys who aren’t his son about it and weirdly, they think it’s cool he hangs out with them and consider him one of the boys. I love my friends and still want to hangout with them, but The dad being around ALL THE TIME is too much. Aita for asking my friend if his dad is going to be there before I agree to hangout with them?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: This is a **1**—**you are absolutely within your rights to ask**, and your boundaries are valid. Here’s why: ### **1. It’s Not Wrong to Set Boundaries** You’re not being rude or unreasonable. Your comfort and social experience matter, especially in a space where you’re introducing your girlfriend (who clearly felt uncomfortable). The fact that some friends normalize his behavior doesn’t mean it’s okay—**your feelings are valid**, and you’re not obligated to tolerate it. ### **2. Context Matters** - **Your home**: You’re the host, and it’s reasonable to expect to know who’s coming over (especially when it’s a surprise). - **Public spaces (clubs, etc.)**: You can’t control who your friends bring, but you can choose whether to engage or leave. If he’s consistently inappropriate, you might need to reconsider how much you expose yourself to him. - **Your girlfriend’s comfort**: If she’s uncomfortable, that’s a red flag. You should prioritize her well-being too. ### **3. The "Locker Room Talk" Issue** His behavior (even if he’s "just joking") is problematic. Normalizing disrespectful talk about women—especially younger ones—isn’t harmless. If your friends defend it, that’s on *them*, not you. You’re not obligated to tolerate that either. ### **4. How to Approach It** If you ask, **"Hey, just checking—will your dad be there this time?"**, it’s a simple, neutral way to gauge. If he says yes, you can decide whether to go or not. If he says no, great—you can still enjoy the hangout. ### **5. Long-Term Considerations** If this keeps happening, you might need to have a **serious conversation with your friend** (privately) about why his dad’s presence is uncomfortable. Frame it as: *"I love hanging out with you and the group, but I’ve noticed [dad’s behavior] makes me uncomfortable. Can we find a way to keep things more chill?"* --- ### **Final Thought** You’re not being petty—you’re being **self-aware and respectful of your own limits**. If your friends can’t understand that, that’s their issue, not yours. **100% valid to ask.** *(P.S. If his dad’s behavior escalates, it’s okay to distance yourself from the group if needed. Your comfort and safety come first.)*
